title: How the Federal Reserve Works
description: Who actually decides U.S. interest rates? In this episode we walk through how the Federal Reserve is built — the Board of Governors, the 12 Reserve Banks, and the FOMC — what it is trying to achieve, how it changes interest rates, and three common misunderstandings. Every fact is taken from the Federal Reserve's own public materials (listed below). Examples marked "Hypothetical example" are illustrations, not real data.

segments.text: Who actually decides interest rates in America? Let's find out.

visual.title: How the Federal Reserve Works
visual.subtitle: Who decides U.S. interest rates — and how

segments.text: When the news says the Fed raised rates or the Fed cut rates, it can sound like one person flipping a switch. It isn't. In this video we'll look at who the Federal Reserve is, who actually votes on interest rates, what the Fed is trying to achieve, and how a decision made in Washington can reach a car loan, a savings account, or a small business. By the end, you should be able to explain the Fed to a friend in about a minute.

visual.heading: What is the Federal Reserve?
items: The central bank of the United States
Created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913
Goal at the start: a monetary system that can respond to stress in the banking system
visual.note: Source: federalreserve.gov, "The Fed Explained — Who We Are"

segments.text: Let's start with the basics. The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It was created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, to establish a monetary system that could respond effectively to stresses in the banking system. A central bank is not the kind of bank where you open a checking account. Its customers are banks and the federal government, and its decisions shape the conditions that every other bank works in.

visual.heading: Five key functions
items: Conducts the nation's monetary policy
Promotes the stability of the financial system
Supervises and regulates financial institutions
Fosters safe and efficient payment and settlement systems
Promotes consumer protection and community development
visual.note: Source: federalreserve.gov, "The Fed Explained — Who We Are"

segments.text: The Fed describes five key functions. It conducts the nation's monetary policy. It promotes the stability of the financial system. It supervises and regulates financial institutions. It fosters the safety and efficiency of the payment and settlement system. And it promotes consumer protection and community development. Interest rates belong to the first one, monetary policy, and that is where most of this video will focus.

board.title: Board of Governors
board.body: Federal agency in Washington, D.C. · 7 governors

banks.title: 12 Reserve Banks
banks.body: Operating arms around the country · 24 Branches

segments.text: The framers of the Federal Reserve Act deliberately did not build a single central bank. They built a system. Today it has three key parts. First, the Board of Governors, a federal agency in Washington, D.C. Second, twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, which are the system's operating arms around the country. And third, the Federal Open Market Committee, usually called the FOMC, which is where interest rate decisions are made. Let's take them one at a time.

visual.heading: The Board of Governors
items: 7 governors, staggered 14-year terms
Nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate
Chair and Vice Chair serve four-year terms and can be reappointed
Reports to, and is directly accountable to, Congress
visual.note: Source: federalreserve.gov, "The Fed Explained — Who We Are"

segments.text: The Board of Governors is the governing body of the system. It has seven members, called governors, who serve staggered fourteen-year terms. Each one is nominated by the President of the United States and confirmed by the Senate. One governor serves as Chair and one as Vice Chair, in four-year terms that can be renewed. The Board guides how the whole system operates, oversees the twelve Reserve Banks, and reports to, and is directly accountable to, Congress. Those long, staggered terms matter: no single election replaces the whole Board at once.

visual.heading: 12 Federal Reserve Banks
visual.note: Each Reserve Bank serves its own district. Source: The Fed Explained (PDF), figure 1.3

segments.text: Next, the twelve Federal Reserve Banks. Each one serves its own district: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas, and San Francisco. Together with their twenty-four branches, they supervise and examine banks, lend to banks to keep cash flowing through the system, distribute currency and coins, help run payment systems, and act as the government's bank by keeping the Treasury's account. They also gather information about their regions, from businesses, banks, and communities, and that information feeds into national policy.
So who actually votes on interest rates? That's the FOMC.

visual.heading: The FOMC: who votes
items: All 7 governors
The president of the New York Fed
4 of the other 11 Reserve Bank presidents, rotating one-year terms
The other 7 presidents attend and join the discussion
Meets at least 8 times a year
visual.note: Source: federalreserve.gov, "The Fed Explained — Who We Are"

segments.text: The Federal Open Market Committee has twelve voting members. All seven governors vote. The president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York always votes. And four of the other eleven Reserve Bank presidents vote, rotating in one-year terms. The presidents who are not voting that year still attend the meetings and take part in the discussion. The committee meets at least eight times a year. After every scheduled meeting it releases a written statement, and the Chair holds a press conference to explain the decision.

visual.heading: What is the Fed trying to achieve?
items: Maximum employment
Stable prices
Inflation goal: 2% over the longer run (PCE price index)
The law also names moderate long-term interest rates
visual.note: Sources: federalreserve.gov "Monetary Policy"; The Fed Explained (PDF)

segments.text: So what is the committee trying to do? Congress gave the Fed two main goals for monetary policy, often called the dual mandate: maximum employment, and stable prices. Maximum employment means the highest level of employment the economy can sustain while keeping inflation stable. For stable prices, the committee has said that inflation of two percent, measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with its mandate over the longer run. The law also lists moderate long-term interest rates as a goal.

left.title: Easing: lower the target range
items: Lower short-term interest rates
Looser financial conditions
May be needed if the economy is sluggish or inflation is too low

right.title: Tightening: raise the target range
items: Higher interest rates
Tighter financial conditions
May be needed if the economy is overheating or inflation is too high

segments.text: The main dial the Fed turns is the federal funds rate, an interest rate for overnight borrowing between banks. More precisely, the FOMC sets a target range for that rate. Lowering the range is called easing. It comes with lower short-term interest rates and looser financial conditions, and it may be needed if the economy is sluggish or inflation is too low. Raising the range is called tightening, and it may be needed if the economy is overheating or inflation is too high.

visual.heading: How the Fed steers the rate
items: Interest on reserve balances
The overnight reverse repurchase facility rate
Sometimes: large-scale asset purchases (quantitative easing)
Sometimes: forward guidance about future policy
visual.note: Source: federalreserve.gov, "The Fed Explained — Monetary Policy"

segments.text: The Fed doesn't simply announce a number and hope. To keep short-term rates inside the target range, it uses tools such as the interest it pays banks on their reserve balances, and the rate on its overnight reverse repurchase facility. At other times it has also used large-scale asset purchases, sometimes called quantitative easing, and forward guidance, which means signaling what it is likely to do in the future.

visual.heading: From a Fed decision to your wallet
steps: Other interest rates and financial conditions usually move
Households and businesses adjust spending and borrowing
Economic activity, jobs, and inflation respond
visual.note: Effects can take several quarters or more. Source: The Fed Explained (PDF)

segments.text: Here is how a decision travels. The committee changes the target range. That change normally affects, and is accompanied by, changes in other interest rates and in financial conditions more broadly. Those changes then influence the spending and borrowing decisions of households and businesses, which in turn affect economic activity, employment, and inflation. Importantly, this is not instant. The Fed itself notes that policy actions may take several quarters or more before their effects on spending and inflation take hold.

visual.heading: A small business deciding whether to borrow
lines: A bakery plans to borrow to buy a second oven.
Before: the loan it is offered costs 8% a year.
After the Fed tightens, suppose lenders offer 9% instead.
Higher monthly payments may lead the owner to wait — one of many small decisions that can slow spending.

segments.text: Let's make that concrete with a hypothetical example. Imagine a bakery that wants to borrow money to buy a second oven. Suppose the loan it is offered costs eight percent a year. After the Fed tightens policy, suppose lenders now offer nine percent instead. Those numbers are made up for illustration. But the logic is real: a higher payment may lead the owner to wait. Multiply that by millions of households and businesses, and you can see how the Fed tries to cool spending when inflation is too high, or encourage it when the economy is weak.
Now, three things people often get wrong about the Fed.

visual.heading: Myth 1: "The Fed is a private company"

left.title: Public side
items: The Board is a federal agency, accountable to Congress
Reserve Banks operate in the public interest, not for shareholders
Net earnings go to the U.S. Treasury

right.title: Private-style features
items: Member banks hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank
They elect six of each Reserve Bank's nine directors
Not funded by congressional appropriations

segments.text: Myth number one: the Fed is a private company. The real answer is a blend. The Board of Governors is a federal agency that is accountable to Congress. The twelve Reserve Banks do have some private-style features: member banks hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank and elect six of its nine directors. But the Fed's own materials stress that Reserve Banks are operated in the public interest, not in the interest of shareholders. The Fed isn't funded by congressional appropriations. It is financed mainly by interest on the securities it owns, and after expenses its net earnings are transferred to the U.S. Treasury.

visual.heading: Myth 2: "The Fed sets my mortgage rate"
items: The FOMC sets a target range for an overnight rate between banks
Mortgage, auto, and card rates are set by lenders and markets
They are often influenced by Fed policy, but are not the same number

segments.text: Myth number two: the Fed sets my mortgage rate. It doesn't, at least not directly. The committee sets a target range for an overnight rate between banks. The rate on your mortgage, car loan, or credit card is set by lenders and by markets. Those rates are often influenced by Fed policy, but they are different numbers, and they can move for other reasons too. We'll dig into exactly how in the next episode.

visual.heading: Myth 3: "The President decides interest rates"
items: Interest rate decisions are made by the FOMC
Congress sets the goals and gave the Fed operational independence
Accountability: public statements, press conferences, testimony to Congress twice a year

segments.text: Myth number three: the President decides interest rates. Rate decisions are made by the FOMC. Congress set the Fed's goals, and it also gave the Fed operational independence, so that decisions can focus on the longer term and rest on data and analysis. In return, the Fed is accountable: it publishes statements after its meetings, the Chair holds press conferences, and twice a year the Chair testifies before Congress.

visual.heading: Recap
items: The Fed is a system: the Board, 12 Reserve Banks, and the FOMC
12 FOMC members vote on monetary policy
Goals: maximum employment and stable prices (2% inflation)
Main tool: the target range for the federal funds rate
Effects travel through other rates, take time, and are not guaranteed

segments.text: Let's recap. The Federal Reserve is a system, not a single bank: a Board of Governors in Washington, twelve Reserve Banks around the country, and the FOMC, where twelve voting members set monetary policy. Its goals are maximum employment and stable prices, with an inflation goal of two percent. Its main tool is the target range for the federal funds rate. And the effects travel through other interest rates and financial conditions, take time, and are never guaranteed.
